Let’s talk about something every pro faces—what I’d call the ongoing battle: dealing with sabotage and setbacks.
You know, there’s this hope that once you finally decide to go all in—once you commit to being a professional—things will just fall into place. But honestly, life rarely cooperates like that. Even after you’ve built your routines and started to settle into that new identity, those old habits? They can still sneak back in.
Maybe you’ve been making steady progress, then out of nowhere, there’s this urge to binge-watch shows for hours. Or you hit a stretch where nothing seems to go your way. For some people, it’s that quiet voice that shows up after a tough critique or a disappointing result, whispering, “Maybe you’re just not cut out for this.” The temptation to slip back into what’s comfortable? It’s strong—sometimes stronger than we expect.
Let me give you a real example. There’s this designer who’d been working steadily for months, and she finally landed a huge client. The excitement was there, but so was the pressure. As the deadline got closer, she caught herself procrastinating, second-guessing every single choice, even picking fights with her friends. It was almost like some part of her wanted to sabotage the very thing she’d worked so hard for. And here’s the thing—this wasn’t the first time she’d done it. She recognized the pattern.
Most of us don’t realize just how deep these self-sabotaging habits can run. They’re often rooted in fear. Not just fear of failure, but sometimes, fear of actual success—or even just the idea of leaving behind the familiar, even if that familiar is a little uncomfortable.
What separates the pro from the amateur? The professional learns to expect these tough moments. Instead of letting setbacks become proof that they’re not good enough, they see them for what they are—reminders that the work actually matters, that the stakes are real.
At some point, it becomes clear: setbacks aren’t a sign you should quit. They’re an invitation to recommit. The pro doesn’t pretend the struggle isn’t there. They face it, tweak their routines if they need to, and most importantly, they keep showing up. And you know what? Over time, those setbacks lose their power. Every time you return to the work, those old patterns start to loosen their grip.
This journey—it’s never just a straight line. There are days filled with doubt, moments when you slip back, and times when the whole thing feels impossible. But here’s the key: these aren’t failures. They’re just part of the process. The real win comes from coming back to the work, again and again, no matter how many times those old habits try to pull you off track.
